research.label: Research target alignment
research.method: For each factor, q = (number of requested labels found at the site) / (number of requested labels). Index = 100 × the weighted mean of q.
assumptions: This index measures how well a site matches your geological targets. It does not measure scientific value, the chance of a discovery or access to samples.
The labels are qualitative descriptions from the literature for the recorded region. A target that is not reported may still be present.
Materials and landforms can overlap in meaning. Their weights are your preferences. They are not independent probabilities.

rover_field_test.label: Regional rover test fit
rover_field_test.method: q = max(0, 1 − |measured regional value − your target| / your tolerance). Index = 100 × the weighted mean of q.
assumptions: The targets of 1 degree (tolerance 5 degrees) and 100 m relief (tolerance 300 m) are example values that you can edit. They are not validated rover limits.
Both terrain values use cells of about 3.7 km. They cannot show rocks, metre-scale slopes, trafficability or how wheels interact with the soil.
The index measures how well the regional environment fits a planned test. It does not measure vehicle performance or safety.

analog_reference.label: Similarity to {mars_name} (Mars)
analog_reference.method: Similarity = 100 / (1 + D). D is the weighted mean of the distances between each Earth site and {mars_name} for each feature. Slope and relief use scaled differences on the same ~3.7 km baseline. Landforms and minerals use the Jaccard distance of the literature labels. Dryness uses the precipitation difference. This is the same calculation as the analog ranking in Explore (spec {analog_version}). Each factor's points show how much of the 100 it cost.
assumptions: The Mars site is the one paired with your mission in Mission Design.

Slope and relief together keep the terrain share from the analog spec. The Earth Low slopes and Less rugged ground sliders only set how it is split between them. Landforms, minerals and dryness keep their analog spec weights.
Elevation and sunlight are not compared. The two planets use different elevation datums, and Mars receives 0.431 of Earth's sunlight (NASA Mars Fact Sheet).

Terrain values use cells of about 3.7 km on both planets. They cannot show rocks, metre-scale slopes or trafficability. Landform and mineral labels come from the literature. They are not spectral measurements.
The index is a rough measure of similarity. It is not a probability or a validated rating of a test site.

base_planning.label: Base-planning evidence review
base_planning.method: There is no overall score. Evidence on infrastructure, resources and hazards is not available.
assumptions: Terrain profiles alone cannot show whether a base is viable.
evidence_gaps: Reliable water/resource quantities and extraction feasibility
Seasonal surface power and energy-storage requirements
Geotechnical bearing capacity and landing-scale hazards
